This remarkably compressed generation time, among the shortest recorded for any pelagic tunicate, reflects the extreme r-selected strategy that defines this species. Individuals reared at this temperature cease swimming and feeding abruptly at the end of their short lives, a pattern of age-related death that appears tied to the physiological collapse following a single, massive burst of reproductive output.

When Oikopleura longicauda is cultured at a higher temperature of 22 °C [T = 22 °C], embryonic development is accelerated considerably, and hatching occurs just 0.33 days [ab = 0.33 days] after fertilisation. This extraordinarily brief embryonic period, lasting less than eight hours, is among the fastest documented for any chordate and is consistent with the minute egg size and simple blastula morphology characteristic of the genus. The timing of this developmental milestone is strongly modulated by thermal conditions, with increasing temperatures compressing the window of organogenesis and yolk-dependent embryo development into a fraction of a day.

As females approach the culmination of their brief reproductive lives, they release a single batch of oocytes through the oviduct before undergoing rapid senescence. This fecundity is achieved without multiple spawning events, as the species is functionally semelparous, investing all available resources into a single, synchronous spawning episode that coincides with the completion of the short adult stage.

The truncated lifespan appears to be a fixed biological constraint rather than a consequence of laboratory artefacts, as field-collected individuals from equatorial waters show similar age-related mortality patterns.

At the elevated rearing temperature of 22 °C [T = 22 °C], the interval between fertilisation and the first feeding larva is extremely short, with the transition to the exotrophic stage occurring only 0.33 days [ab = 0.33 days] post-fertilisation.
